text: To enshrine something is to fix it somewhere protected and permanent — a shrine is where you keep sacred things — treating it as too important to casually undo. Roberts's point is that birthright citizenship isn't just an ordinary rule: it was enshrined in the Constitution itself in 1868, which makes it about as hard to remove as American law allows.

To contravene a law, rule, or ruling is to act in conflict with it — to go against something already settled. Trump's order seemed to contravene an 1898 Supreme Court decision that had answered this exact question over a century ago, which is a big part of why lower courts blocked it so fast.

A revisionist view re-writes the accepted version of history or facts, usually to support a new argument — and calling something revisionist is often a polite way of saying the rewrite is bogus. That's how Roberts uses it: the administration claimed everyone had misread the 14th Amendment for over a century, and he answers that there's “scant evidence” for such a dramatic do-over.

To rebuff is to reject something sharply and decisively — to turn it back cold, the way you might rebuff an offer to copy someone's homework. The decision rebuffs Trump's attempt flat-out: no compromise, no middle ground, just no.

To curtail something is to cut it back or limit it — trim it shorter than it was, like curtailing recess to twenty minutes. Trump wasn't trying to abolish birthright citizenship entirely, just shrink who it covers; the Court said he couldn't do even that.

A bid here is an attempt — a serious try at getting something — not an offer of money at an auction. “Trump's bid to curtail birthright citizenship” just means his push to make it happen, and the headline is announcing that the bid failed.

A birthright is something you're entitled to simply by being born, so birthright citizenship is the rule that being born on U.S. soil automatically makes you a U.S. citizen — no application, no test, no matter who your parents are. It's the whole subject of this case, and the Court just confirmed it stays.

When a court strikes down a law or order, it cancels it — declares it invalid so it simply stops existing as law. It's the courts' heaviest hammer, and this article has the Supreme Court swinging it at Trump's policies twice: the citizenship order here, and his tariff program back in February.

A crackdown is a sudden get-tough campaign of strict enforcement — authorities “cracking down” the way a teacher might crack down on phones in class. The article calls this order Trump's most aggressive crackdown on illegal immigration.

To upend something is to flip it upside down — and figuratively, to completely overturn how things have always worked. Ending automatic citizenship for children born here would have upended an understanding Americans have relied on since 1868.

Deep-rooted means anchored so firmly and for so long that it's extremely hard to pull out — like a tree whose roots go down for decades. The understanding that birth on American soil means citizenship has had more than 150 years to grow those roots.

Virtually here means “almost entirely” — nothing to do with computers or virtual reality. “Virtually everyone born on American soil” means nearly everyone, with only rare exceptions like the children of foreign diplomats.

“Soil” in this phrase means territory, not dirt — being “born on American soil” means being born anywhere inside the United States. Lawyers and journalists love the expression because it makes the rule vivid: the ground you're born on decides your citizenship.

The Chief Justice is the head judge of the Supreme Court — one of the nine justices, but the one who leads the Court and often writes its biggest opinions. John Roberts has held the job since 2005, and he wrote this ruling himself.

The Framers are the people who “framed” — drafted and built — the Constitution and its amendments. When Roberts writes that “the Framers of the Fourteenth Amendment extended that promise,” he's reaching back to the lawmakers of 1868 and saying today's Court is keeping their word.

A justice is a judge on a supreme court — the U.S. Supreme Court has nine of them, appointed for life. Here they split six against Trump's order and three in favor, which is why the article keeps counting them.

To dissent is to formally disagree — on a court, a justice who dissents votes against the majority and usually writes an opinion explaining why. A dissent doesn't change the outcome, but it goes on the record; Alito's angry one here calls the ruling “a serious mistake.”

Grounds here means reasons or legal basis — not a place. Ruling “on constitutional grounds” means the justices based their decision on the Constitution itself; the article notes only five of the six did, because Kavanaugh got to the same result by a different route.

An executive order is a written command the president issues alone — no vote in Congress needed. That makes it fast but fragile: because it's only the president's own directive, courts can strike it down if it conflicts with a law or the Constitution, which is exactly what happened here.

When a rule “takes effect,” it starts actually applying to people. This order never took effect at all — judges froze it almost immediately — so no baby ever actually lost citizenship under it while the courts fought it out.

An amendment added to the Constitution in 1868, just after the Civil War, mainly to guarantee citizenship and equal legal protection to freed slaves. Its opening sentence — everyone “born or naturalized in the United States” is a citizen — is the exact text this whole case was fought over.

To be naturalized is to become a citizen of a country you weren't born in, by going through the official process — living there legally, passing a test, taking an oath. The 14th Amendment covers both doors into citizenship: born here, or naturalized here.

Jurisdiction is the reach of a government's legal authority — who its laws and courts have power over. The amendment's phrase “subject to the jurisdiction thereof” (old legal-speak for “of it”) means people U.S. law actually governs, and the fight was over exactly who that clause leaves out.

To appeal a court decision is to ask a higher court to review and overturn it — losing in a lower court isn't the end if you can climb the ladder. The administration appealed its losses all the way up to the Supreme Court, which is the top rung; there's nowhere to appeal after this.

To contend is to argue or claim something forcefully, especially in a dispute. The administration was contending that everyone had misunderstood the 14th Amendment for more than a century — a bold claim, and the one the Court rejected.

In law, a provision is one specific clause or section of a document — not supplies for a trip. The “citizenship provision” is the particular sentence of the 14th Amendment that grants citizenship by birth.

The drafters of a law are the people who wrote it — a “draft” is a working version of a text. The administration's argument hinged on what the drafters of 1868 meant: protecting former slaves' children, it claimed, not the children of people here illegally.

“Birth tourism” is traveling to a country specifically to give birth there, so the baby is born a citizen. Trump used it as his justification for narrowing the rule; Alito's dissent complains that the ruling protects even the children of “birth tourists.”

Scant means barely any — a scant amount is so small it hardly counts. When Roberts says there is “scant evidence” for the administration's reading of history, it's a judge's dry way of saying: you showed up nearly empty-handed.

A flank is the side of an army in battle formation, and writers borrow the word for the wings of a group. The court's “right flank” is its most conservative side — Thomas, Alito, and Gorsuch — the three justices who dissented.

To confer something is to grant or bestow it, usually something valuable like a degree, an honor, or a right. Alito's complaint is that, as the Court reads it, the amendment confers citizenship on virtually everyone born here — hands it out automatically, in his view too freely.

Adoption here means the process of officially approving something and making it part of the law — nothing to do with adopting a child. “The process that led to its adoption” means the debates and votes by which the 14th Amendment was added to the Constitution.

When a court decides a case, the side with the most votes writes the majority opinion — the official explanation that becomes binding law. Here Roberts wrote it, four justices signed on fully, and the dissenters attacked it; “the majority” is shorthand for the winning side.

An appointee is someone chosen — appointed — for a position by whoever has the power to pick. Supreme Court justices are presidential appointees who serve for life, which is why it stings that Barrett and Kavanaugh, both Trump appointees, ruled against the president who chose them.

To enact is to turn a bill into an official law — the moment it stops being a proposal and starts being enforceable. Kavanaugh's twist: he said the order didn't violate the Constitution, but it did break a federal law Congress first enacted in 1940.

A politician's platform is the set of positions and promises they campaign on — the ideas they “stand on,” like a speaker on a stage. Curtailing birthright citizenship was a key plank of Trump's 2024 immigration platform; no software or stage involved.

Unprecedented means never done before — there's no earlier example (no “precedent”) to point to. In the entire history of the country, no sitting president had ever come to watch a Supreme Court argument in person until Trump showed up for this one in April.

A “sitting” president is one currently in office — sitting in the seat of power right now, as opposed to a former or future one. Plenty of ex-presidents have visited the Court; a sitting one attending an argument had never happened.

In court, a hearing is a formal session where judges listen to the two sides make their cases — the Supreme Court “hearing arguments” means the justices sitting and listening to the lawyers, not overhearing something. This is the session Trump showed up to watch.

“The high court” is just another name for the Supreme Court — the highest court in the country, sitting above all the lower courts whose rulings it can review. Journalists use it to avoid repeating “Supreme Court” in every sentence.

A politician's “signature” policies are their defining ones — the projects so identified with them it's as if their name were signed on each. This ruling is the third time this year the Court has blocked one of Trump's signature initiatives, after the tariffs and the Federal Reserve firing.

A tariff is a tax a country charges on goods coming in from abroad, usually to protect its own industries or pressure other countries. Trump's global tariff program was another of his big policies — and in February, the Court struck that one down too.

To denounce someone is to attack them publicly and harshly — to condemn them out loud, not just disagree quietly. After the tariff ruling, Trump denounced the justices who ruled against him as unintelligent and disloyal.

America's central bank — “the Fed” — which sets interest rates and steers the money supply, run by a board of governors designed to be independent of politics. On Monday the Court stopped Trump from firing one of those governors, the second big loss mentioned alongside this one.

To be entitled to something is to have a legal right to it — it's owed to you, not a favor. The 1898 decision confirmed that U.S.-born children of immigrants are entitled to citizenship: they don't have to ask for it, it's already theirs.

A ruling is a court's official decision on a question. The lower-court rulings all went against Trump's order, the administration appealed them, and the Supreme Court's ruling here is the final word — there's no court above it.

A visa is official permission to enter and stay in a country for a set purpose and time — a student visa, a tourist visa. Trump's order targeted babies born to parents here illegally or on temporary visas — people allowed in, but only as visitors.
